name: Compton Scattering
description: A 100 keV X-ray photon scatters off a free electron, transferring some of its energy

layman.title: Light Bounces Off Matter
layman.summary: Watch what happens when a photon collides with an electron and bounces away with less energy

sections.whatsHappening: A high-energy photon is heading toward an electron. Unlike absorption (where the photon vanishes entirely), here the photon bounces off the electron like a billiard ball. The photon loses some energy in the collision and changes direction, while the electron gets knocked away. The photon keeps going but with less energy than before.
sections.whyItMatters: Compton scattering proved that light really does behave like a particle, not just a wave. This was one of the key experiments that launched quantum mechanics. It is also the main way X-rays interact with soft tissue in medical imaging; the scattered X-rays fog the image, so X-ray machines use grids to block them.
sections.whatToWatch: Follow the yellow photon as it approaches the electron. At impact, the photon turns 90° and the electron is knocked forward and down at about 40°. Notice the photon's wave trail: after scattering, its waves are about 20% longer, because its energy dropped from 100 keV to 83.6 keV.
sections.funFact: Arthur Compton won the Nobel Prize in 1927 for this discovery. In 1923 he aimed X-rays from a molybdenum target at graphite and found the scattered X-rays had longer wavelengths, exactly as his billiard-ball calculation predicted.

scientific.narrative: A 100 keV photon scatters through θ = 90° off an electron treated as free and at rest. The Compton formula gives the scattered photon energy E′ = 83.63 keV, so its wavelength grows from 12.40 pm to 14.82 pm (Δλ = λ_C = 2.43 pm at 90°). The electron carries away the difference, 16.37 keV of kinetic energy, moving at 0.247c at 39.9° from the photon's original direction, as momentum conservation requires. The wavelength shift depends only on the scattering angle, not on the initial photon energy.

equations.label: Compton wavelength shift
equations.tex: Δλ = λ′ - λ = (h/m_e c)(1 - cos θ)

equations.label: Scattered photon energy
equations.tex: E′ = E / (1 + (E/m_e c²)(1 - cos θ)) = 83.63 keV

equations.label: Electron recoil angle
equations.tex: cot φ = (1 + E/m_e c²) tan(θ/2), φ = 39.9°

constants: Incident photon: 100 keV (hard X-ray), λ = 12.40 pm

simplifications: The electron is treated as free and at rest. A real atomic electron is bound, but its binding energy (13.6 eV in hydrogen) is negligible next to the 16.4 keV it receives.
